analysis.one_liner: Funds free lawyers for low-income tenants facing eviction in states and cities that pass right-to-counsel laws.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on July 25, 2025 and has received no further action, with no committee vote or floor vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an Eviction Right to Counsel Fund at HUD, authorized at $100 million a year for five years. States, cities, and tribal governments could get grants if they pass laws guaranteeing free, full legal representation to tenants earning up to 200% of the federal poverty level who are facing eviction or loss of a housing subsidy. Extra priority would go to jurisdictions that also limit no-fault evictions, require 30 days' notice, run eviction diversion programs, or provide emergency rental assistance.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income tenants — those earning up to 200% of the poverty line — facing eviction or termination of a housing subsidy in states and cities that enact right-to-counsel laws. Most tenants in eviction cases today face their landlord's lawyer alone, and representation sharply improves the odds a tenant keeps their housing.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a $100 million-a-year grant fund for fiscal years 2026-2030 to reimburse state, local, and tribal governments for the cost of providing free legal representation to tenants in eviction and subsidy-termination cases.
Covers tenants with incomes at or below 200% of the federal poverty line, and covers both evictions and the termination of a housing subsidy.
Grants only go to governments that enact right-to-counsel legislation, so the federal money rewards jurisdictions that guarantee the representation by their own law.

HUD must prioritize applicants that also limit no-fault evictions, require at least 30 days' written notice before eviction, run eviction diversion programs, or provide emergency rental assistance, and that use funds to train and recruit eviction defense attorneys.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the $500 million authorization over five years, and landlords in participating jurisdictions face tenants with lawyers in eviction court, which makes filings to force tenants out slower and more expensive.

drawbacks.text: The fund is only $100 million a year nationwide, which is small relative to eviction caseloads — millions of eviction cases are filed annually in the U.S. — so it would cover only a fraction of eligible tenants even in participating jurisdictions.
The grants are opt-in: the bill cannot force any state or city to pass a right-to-counsel law, so tenants in jurisdictions that decline would get nothing from it.
Defenders of landlords argue that giving tenants lawyers raises landlords' legal costs and delays removing nonpaying tenants, costs that can push small landlords to raise rents or sell.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is real but narrow: a federally funded lawyer can be the difference between keeping and losing a home in eviction court, and studies of existing local right-to-counsel programs show represented tenants far more often stay housed. The cost is modest relative to federal budgets — $500 million over five years — but the design is voluntary and the funding level is small, so national impact would be limited even if it passed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote as of the latest record.

narrative.text: Representative Summer Lee introduced the bill on July 25, 2025, with seven original cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, the only committee referral in its action history.
Eleven members have cosponsored the bill, all Democrats.
The bill has no further actions: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action since its referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened yet, the bill has not changed anyone's position; tenants and landlords remain under existing state law, and no funds have been authorized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet — the bill sits in committee

sides.party_line_note: All 12 supporters of the bill, including the sponsor and every cosponsor, are Democrats, and no Republican has joined; with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill has not advanced in the Judiciary Committee.

industries.note: The bill does not directly regulate landlords, but by funding lawyers for tenants it makes evictions slower and costlier in participating jurisdictions, including cases against tenants who have not paid rent. Tenant advocates see representation as correcting a mismatch where landlords appear with counsel and tenants almost never do; landlord groups generally oppose right-to-counsel mandates as raising their costs.

industries.industry: Eviction defense and legal aid attorneys
industries.note: The bill directs grant funds toward training and recruiting attorneys to represent tenants, creating paid work that goes hand in hand with the benefit to tenants.

Local governments can receive federal money to offset the cost of a new service obligation, but accepting it means adopting an ongoing right-to-counsel commitment the federal grant may not fully cover after 2030.

analysis.trajectory: With a Democratic-only cosponsor list, no Republican support, and no committee action months after referral, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote in this Congress; it will most likely die quietly in committee unless there is a major shift in House control or the bill is folded into a larger housing package.
